chapter: Bands and bandleading in New Orleans
title: Parade of Bands on WDSU television, 1952-53
summary: Bergen tells of getting the Barnett Furniture show, the bass breaking on air, the dry mouth, bad microphone placement, and Blind Gilbert as guest.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Well, there was a man in the advertising business, Dick. His name was John...I can't think of his last name. John what? John Curran. No, uh-huh. Anyway, he was Shep Morrison's brother-in-law. Big old fella. Nice guy. And he gave me a ring about one o'clock in the day and said he needed a band or a try-off at WDSU. Parade of Bands. That was the name of the program was the Parade of Bands sponsored by Barnett Furniture Company. So, I told him I sure would. I'd like to play it. I get on the phone. I can't get in touch with Tom Brown. I can't get in touch with a couple other guys. So, I introduced myself over the phone to Digger Lane. I said, Digger, you don't know me but I know you and I got a good deal coming up and we make the grade. I said, can you be at WDSU about three feet? And I lined the band up. Jake Chambry on piano. Sherwood wasn't doing anything. I got Sherwood, Charlie Fabright and Ram and Booth. While we go down there and naturally I called tunes that we all knew and it seemed to go over pretty good, Dick. And I told Johnny, I keep saying Johnny Conley, it wasn't Conley though, his name wasn't Conley. And he was timing the tunes as we played them and before you knew it we had the schedule all made up. He said, the job is yours. And we go the next night to play. And of course, it never did happen before in his life but while he was playing Sherwood Man Japan's the bridge and his bass fiddle breaks. And then he thought, during the commercial, he thought the camera was pointing one way and he walked right behind him with his bass fiddle doing a commercial. It looked good though, that was a good kick. We didn't know it and he didn't know it so I guess he did the right thing. He had to get the bass fiddle fixed. And with the extreme air conditioning there, right in the middle of a chorus my mouth went so dry I could hardly play. And just lucky I got through that chorus and I had to have a glass of water concealed in the room so I could take a sip of it every once in a while when the camera was off of me. And there was only one bad thing about that. It could have maybe helped me to climb the ladder a little bit but whoever was in charge of that program at that time, they were more interested in concealing the microphone to make the picture look good than in the quality of music they were putting out. So you know yourself when you see me play I usually hold the horn up about on a fifteen degree angle towards the ceiling. Well they put a microphone right by my belt buckle. And I was blowing loud that night. I mean I was blowing so loud that one guy said, can you cut it down a little bit, they're rehearsing in the next studio. Now this is when we were broadcasting. So I was just tickled to death that I sounded so strong you know. And when Raymond plays he usually bends down and Raymond was playing harmony to me right in the microphone. And I was blowing up to the ceiling over the mic. And Diggalane he played down on the other side right in the microphone. Well when I got home and one of my friends said, what's the matter with you? You're weak. We could hardly hear you. Oh man that broke my heart almost. Because I was blowing. If he had a boom, a boom mic about five or ten foot away from me I would have blasted the place out. And one of my friends taped that program for me and when I got home and I heard it, I still have it. Unless I'm playing by myself, even when I play by myself the tone is dead. You know, coming off the back wall. The wall was about thirty feet away from us, the back wall. And it was one of the biggest disappointments of my life, in spite of the fact that I don't think I made any clinkers at all, and I was very nervous. And the band wasn't too bad. Raymond played good, Diggal played good. I played my heart out. The rhythm section was all right. But the trumpet had a dull, dead tone to it when you could hear it. The reception was real bad. And those boys, if I had anything against them, which I know it was just tough luck, but they got even with me if they had anything against me. But I know they did. It was just a case of the technicians wearing on the ball. But everything went all right and we got through it. Oh, incidentally, guess who my guest artist was on that program? Blind Gilbert. Oh, really? Yeah, I have him on that tape. He sang After You're Gone, as one of our friends would say, After You're Gone. You know what I mean?

It sounded like a street in a French quarter. Not do, man. He was gone. And he takes a break, one of those goofus breaks, and he plays his guitar. We're still talking about Blind Gilbert. And he did all right. We made a little extra life to the program. So that was back in 1951 or 1952, Dick, I guess. About 52.
You got 53 down on this piece of paper.
A half an hour show there. Yeah.
This is real. I just got a minute on it.
So why don't I run this off and put on a new one before we get into anything else? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
